title: Why Feedback Cultures Win
author: Andrea Chiarelli
summary: Chiarelli (with Melissa Muth Martinez) argues that most organisations say they value feedback but never build the habit, so feedback stays an annual event and burnout grows in the resulting silence. She contrasts small teams, where feedback depends on the founder's personality, with large ones, where it is buried under ritualised process. Her remedy is not a new framework but better questions asked regularly and acted on. She offers three: what one thing could I do differently next week, what is getting in your way, and what feedback would you give your manager. The move is to shift leaders from passively saying they are open to feedback to actively requesting it, making feedback a reflex rather than a policy.
points: Feedback culture fails for a structural reason, not apathy: nobody has built the daily habit, so feedback is reserved for annual reviews and retros.
Small and large organisations fail in opposite ways: small teams lack shared language and structure, large ones lack frequency and authenticity.
Saying I am open to feedback is passive; asking What feedback do you have for me is a different posture that signals real listening.
Three recurring questions (next week, what is in your way, feedback for your manager) build the rhythm of feedback into daily work.
Skip-level feedback only works as a repeatable quarterly process with clear confidentiality, and only if leaders visibly act on what they hear.
quotes: In most workplaces, feedback is treated like a special event, reserved for annual reviews, performance interventions or awkward end-of-project retros. It’s not woven into the rhythm of daily work.
Burnout doesn’t come from overwork alone. It comes from working in a vacuum, without feedback, recognition or connection.
Saying “I’m open to feedback” is easy, but it’s passive, and probably won’t lead to anything substantive. It’s like saying, “I’m willing to talk to customers if they walk into my office.
But don’t mistake small for healthy. In many small teams, feedback depends entirely on the founder’s personality or a manager’s instincts.
The annual review becomes a box-ticking exercise. Feedback is delivered as a sandwich, delayed by layers of hierarchy, or “stored up” to rot for end-of-quarter conversations.
You should definitely expect silence at first. People aren’t used to being asked what’s hard, or what might be limiting for them right now.

This question breaks hierarchy without breaking trust. When a manager’s manager asks this with sincerity and receives the answer without defensiveness, it transforms the power dynamic and cuts through the noise.
